column4: This ayah reports a clear victory granted to the Prophet; 48:2 connects that gift to completing favor and guiding him on a straight path.
The section's root ن ع م names a favor completed; here يُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُ is paired with يَهْدِيَكَ صِرَاطًا مُسْتَقِيمًا, joining completion to straight-way guidance.
The section's dictionary wording for رَحْمَة describes a tenderness that issues in doing good; this ayah says God has prescribed mercy for Himself toward creation.
The section treats mercy as the source of beneficence; here God's encompassing mercy is written for those who fear Him, give zakat, and believe in His signs.
The section's wording for mercy explains it as a source of good; this ayah calls the Prophet's mission itself mercy to all worlds.
The section's wording “complete the favor” and its path image meet in لِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي and لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ; the immediate scene is facing the Sacred Mosque.
The section's root ن ع م concerns a bestowed, completed good; this ayah says the religion is perfected and the favor completed, grounding the image in a communal gift.
The section links a received favor to its response; after purification instructions this ayah says God wills to complete His favor and that the people may be grateful.
The section describes ربّ as completing and setting a favor right; this ayah calls the Scripture completion of favor, and also names clarification, guidance, and mercy.
The section says the favor in 1:7 belongs to a people; this promise uses يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ for Joseph and Jacob's family, after choosing Joseph and teaching interpretation.
The section joins received favor, gratitude, choosing, and the straight path; this description of Abraham places شَاكِرًا before choosing and guidance to صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ.
The section's wording in 1:7 is “those You favored”; this ayah names prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and righteous people as those God favored, and makes them companions.
This ayah promises guidance to a straight path; 4:69 identifies the favored people reached by that promise, making the section's favor-and-path pairing concrete.

The section's dictionary wording for minnah includes holding a favor over someone; this ayah rejects converts' claim that their Islam is a favor to the Messenger and calls guidance to faith God's favor.

The section's wording for a favor held over its recipient is staged directly: Moses calls Pharaoh's claimed upbringing “a favor you remind me of” (نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ), against Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel.
The section contrasts recounting a giver's good with reproaching its recipient; this ayah says charity is emptied by مَنًّا or injury, and promises reward without fear to those who refrain.
The section's dictionary sense of minnah as reproach matches this warning not to void charity with مَنًّا or hurt; the comparison is a giver seeking public display.
The section contrasts receiving good with having it held over one; these feeders say they seek neither reward nor thanks (وَلَا شُكُورًا), so the benefit is not turned into a claim on recipients.
The section pictures good passing from one hand to another; this person gives wealth to purify himself, specifying an act of giving as a response to what one has received.
The section's dictionary wording for minnah concerns a favor charged to its recipient; after describing a giver, this ayah says no one's favor is owed back to him (نِعْمَةٍ تُجْزَى).
The section has the recipient answer the giver's good with praise; this neighbor completes the giving passage by naming the giver's pleasure as the donor's aim.
After rejecting repayment for a favor in 92:19, this ayah gives the donor's outcome as satisfaction, contrasting freely given good with indebtedness.
The section's dictionary wording for minnah includes a favor held over someone; this command, وَلَا تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ, bars giving in order to demand more.
The section begins with hamd and ends with a path of favor; the people of Paradise say praise to God who guided them to this, so guidance itself is named as the gift.
The section's opening hamd is repeated here as the final call of Paradise: “praise to Allah, Lord of the worlds” (ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ), after salvation and entry into peace.
After the Queen's throne arrives, Solomon calls it a favor from his Lord and a test of gratitude or denial; the gift is credited to its giver rather than claimed as one's own.
The section's recipient answers a favor with praise; Solomon asks to be enabled to thank the favor bestowed on him and his parents and to do righteous work pleasing God.
The section describes recounting a giver's good among others; this command says to proclaim the favor of your Lord (بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ), using the same favor-and-Rabb wording.
The section treats favor as good conveyed to a recipient; this neighbor says God found Muhammad in need and made him self-sufficient, the concrete favor that 93:11 tells him to proclaim.
The section's image of a good passed to another has an ethical consequence here: after recalling the orphaned Prophet's need, the neighbor forbids oppressing an orphan.
This neighbor forbids repelling a petitioner; alongside the section's account of giving and receiving good, it shows how the recipient of care treats another asker.
The section presents worship as the response to provision and safety; this command tells Quraysh to worship the Lord of this House, and 106:4 names what He supplied.
The section's favor is a good delivered to recipients; this ayah names the provision itself—food against hunger and security against fear—as the reason for 106:3's worship.
The section says hamd recounts a giver's goods; this ayah says God gave people what they asked and that His blessings cannot be counted (لَا تُحْصُوهَا), while naming human injustice and ingratitude.
The section's root ن ع م names bestowed good; this ayah says that if God's نعمة is counted it cannot be enumerated, sharpening the section's image of praise as recounting favors.
The section joins a gift to the recipient's answer; here gratitude (شَكَرْتُمْ) brings increase, while denial of favor (كَفَرْتُمْ) meets punishment.
The section joins a completed gift, guidance, and a grateful response; this fasting passage says to complete the number, glorify God for guiding you, and be grateful.
The section's wording “favor” becomes a shared social event here: God's favor joined former enemies' hearts into brothers and saved them from the edge of a pit of Fire.
The section treats guidance as a favor given to a people; this ayah calls the Messenger's recitation, purification, and teaching a favor to believers who had been in manifest error.
After 4:69 names the people favored by God, this ayah says their companionship is فضل from God, identifying the promised company as gift rather than entitlement.
This command to remember God's favor and covenant, including the people's “we hear and obey,” makes public recollection answerable to obedience, as the section's favor and path are joined.
This command recalls God's favor when hostile people reached toward the believers and God restrained their hands; the received protection is a concrete good that calls for trust.
Moses tells his people to remember God's favor, including making prophets and giving them what was not given to others; the favor is narrated to its recipients.
God reminds Jesus of His favor by listing support, teaching, and protection; this is a concrete example of a giver recounting specific goods to their recipient.
Moses tells Israel to remember God's favor when He saved them from Pharaoh's people and their torment; this names a deliverance behind the section's received-favor image.
The section presents the giver's good as something remembered; this ayah explicitly tells people to remember God's favor and the Book and wisdom sent down to them.
The section pictures a good delivered from a giver to recipients; here cloud shade, manna, and quail are provided to Israel, with the command to eat good things.
This address recounts rescue from an enemy, the appointment at the mountain, and provision of manna and quail; the gifts are followed by a warning not to transgress.
The section's transfer of good to recipients has a communal parallel: God sheltered and strengthened the believers when few and afraid, then provided good things for them.
The section's root ن ع م names bestowed good; this ayah says every نعمة is from God, then contrasts that source with people calling to Him only when harm touches them.
The section opposes praise of a giver to a favor held over its recipient; here people recognize God's favor (يَعْرِفُونَ نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ) and then deny it.
The section links a good provision to its recipient's response; this command to eat lawful, good provision says to be grateful for God's favor if they worship Him.
This ayah names sea-food, ornaments, ships, and seeking God's bounty, then calls for gratitude; it makes material provision a specific instance of the section's bestowed good.
A secure, provisioned town denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; this reversal shows the boundary between receiving a favor and denying its giver.
The section names worship as a response to the giver; Abraham tells idolaters to seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks to Him.
This ayah contrasts the sanctuary's safety and provision with the surrounding people being snatched away, then says its inhabitants deny God's favor; it parallels 106:3–4's safety and food.
The people of Saba are told to eat their Lord's provision and be grateful in a good land; this ties a received, visible good to the response developed in the section.
After Saba's call to gratitude in 34:15, turning away is answered by a flood that replaces their gardens; the reversal marks what denial does to provision.
This ayah names the destruction as recompense for disbelief; following the lost gardens of 34:16, it completes the boundary between favor received and favor denied.
The section pictures a benefit reaching a recipient; this ayah says people eat fruit from what their hands did not make and asks whether they will be grateful.
The section describes recounting the giver's good; travelers are told to remember their Lord's favor when mounted and to glorify Him for subjecting the vehicle.
This continuation supplies the words spoken after remembering the favor in 43:13: “to our Lord we will surely return,” placing the received ride in the larger return to its giver.
This ayah says the sea was subjected so ships sail by God's command and people seek His bounty; it connects provision to the giver and beneficiary.
After the subjected sea and heavens and earth in 45:12, this ayah names that subjection as signs for people who reflect, extending the section's account of received goods.
The section's gift is something received from another; after asking who sends drinking water, this ayah says God could make it bitter and asks why people are not grateful.
This command to be grateful to God makes explicit the recipient's answer to a giver; it says whoever gives thanks benefits himself, while God remains rich and praiseworthy.
David and Solomon say praise belongs to God who favored them over many believing servants; this is the section's public recounting of a giver's favor made explicit.
Abraham praises God for granting him Ishmael and Isaac in old age; the specific family gift is voiced as hamd, the recipient's answer in the section.
After rescue aboard the ship, Noah is told to say praise to God who saved them from the wrongdoing people; the benefit and hamd are joined as in the section.
This opening praise is for God who sent the Scripture to His servant without deviation; it links hamd to a received, straightening guidance.
Asked who sends rain and revives the earth, the answer is Allah; the ayah then says praise belongs to Him, making provision the stated ground of praise.
Those entering Paradise praise God for fulfilling His promise and giving them the earth to inherit; the section's hamd-as-response is tied to a completed gift.
This ayah distinguishes a grateful response, which God approves, from ingratitude, which He does not; it makes the section's recipient-response boundary explicit.
When harm leaves and a person tastes favor, this ayah says he forgets the One he called before; it reverses the section's hamd that keeps the giver in view.
The section's favor is acknowledged by hamd, while this ayah says a person turns away when given favor and despairs when touched by harm, reversing that response.
This ayah contrasts a person's response to harm and favor: he turns away when blessed and becomes wide in supplication when harmed, the inverse of remembering the giver.
After tasting mercy, a person rejoices, but hardship from what his hands sent makes him ungrateful; this makes the section's grateful response a meaningful boundary.
When a person is made to taste mercy and it is withdrawn, this ayah describes despair and ingratitude, a reversal of the section's received good answered by hamd.
This ayah says God does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves; it makes the section's completed favor conditional on the recipients' course.
The section's favor is good from a giver; this ayah describes people exchanging God's favor for disbelief and bringing their people to ruin, the clearest reversal of grateful reception.
These people promise charity and righteousness if God gives them bounty; the next ayah shows the promised response failing, contrasting the section's answer of praise with conditional thanks.
After bounty is given, these people withhold it and turn away; this neighbor completes 9:75's unkept promise and displays the opposite of a recipient's faithful response.
This ayah names hypocrisy and its lasting consequence after the broken promise in 9:75–76, completing the boundary between receiving good and answering it truthfully.
The section joins a bestowed favor to a guided path; this ayah says God showed the way and the human response is either grateful or ungrateful.
The section asks for a straight path of favor; this ayah says God showed the human being two paths, making the choice and possible deviation explicit.
The section's root ن ع م names good bestowed on a recipient; this ayah says people will be asked about النَّعِيم, making received ease answerable.
The section's dictionary sense of أَنْعَمَ includes giving more; this opening says the Prophet was given abundant good (الْكَوْثَرَ), a concentrated instance of gift before response.
After the abundant gift in 108:1, this command directs prayer and sacrifice to the Lord, specifying the recipient's worshipful answer.
Following abundant good and worship in 108:1–2, the opponent is called cut off; this boundary contrasts a granted, lasting good with its opposite.
After victory and people entering God's religion, this command tells the Prophet to glorify his Lord with praise and seek forgiveness, placing hamd after a public gift.
This command to eat good provision and thank God for it makes explicit the recipient's response to a provider, as the section links favor and hamd.
Rain and crops are provided as sustenance, and people are told not to set up rivals to God; the ayah makes the giver behind received good explicit.
The command to Israel to remember the favor bestowed on them directly matches the section's account of recounting a giver's good to its recipients.
This repeated command to remember God's favor to Israel addresses the receiving people as a group, matching the section's plural “those You favored.”
This ayah again tells Israel to remember the favor bestowed on them; its direct act of communal recollection matches the section's recounting of good.
Believers are told to remember God's favor when armies came and God sent wind and unseen forces against them; the favor is a specific rescue narrated to its recipients.
The command to remember God's favor precedes the question who provides from heaven and earth; it directs attention from provision back to its giver.
This ayah calls earlier prophets people God favored; when His signs are recited they fall in prostration and weeping, a bodily response to the bestowed favor and guidance.
This ayah says God chose and guided a line of prophets and their kin to a straight path; it gives a concrete family of recipients for the section's favored people.
After naming prophets and their guidance, this command says to follow their guidance; it makes the section's favored path something walked, not only received.
This ayah says God made leaders who guide by His command and directs them to good deeds, prayer, and almsgiving; it develops guidance as an enacted way.
After God restored life to a people who had fled death, this ayah says God has favor over people but most are ungrateful; it joins a delivered good to its denied response.
God's unequal distribution of provision is followed by the question whether recipients deny His favor; this makes the giver's provision and human acknowledgment explicit.
Spouses, children, and good provision are named as gifts from God, followed by a question about believing falsehood and denying His favor.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then gives hearing, sight, and hearts so they may be grateful; this is a specific bestowed capacity and response.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are attributed to God, yet people give little thanks; the ayah directly contrasts received capacities with the response described in the section.
After forming the human and giving hearing, sight, and hearts, this ayah says how little people are grateful; it names gifts and their deficient answer.
This ayah says God poured out favors, outward and inward, while some dispute about Him; it makes the gifts visible and the response contested.
David's family is told to work in gratitude, yet few of God's servants are grateful; it turns the section's recipient response into sustained service.
Fresh water, food, ornaments, and ships are described as gifts people use to seek God's bounty; this gives material detail to the section's bestowed good.
Winds bring good news, ships sail by God's command, people seek bounty, and may be grateful; provision and gratitude are explicitly joined.
Ships are made still or allowed to sail by God's signs, for every patient and grateful person; it relates a provided means to a grateful recipient.
In a ship at sea people call on God alone, then associate partners after rescue; this sharply reverses acknowledgment of the giver after receiving safety.
People call God alone amid a storm, promise gratitude if saved, then forget after rescue; the passage contrasts a claimed response with received mercy.
After God removes harm, people associate others with Him; the reversal shows how a recipient can conceal the giver after receiving relief.
When harm touches people they call on their Lord, but some associate partners after tasting mercy; this is a specific reversal of the section's praise of the giver.
This ayah calls God possessor of favor over people, then says most do not give thanks; it states both the bestowed good and the failed response.
After people assign part of God's creation to Him, the ayah calls the human plainly ungrateful; it contrasts crediting the giver with misattributing what was received.
A mature person asks to thank God's favor on himself and his parents and to do righteous work pleasing Him; it explicitly joins received good, gratitude, and action.
God promises believers doubled mercy, light, and forgiveness; this is a specific gift of guidance and mercy from the giver named in the section.
This ayah says all bounty is in God's hand and He gives it to whom He wills, denying people control over the favor they might claim as their own.
The ayah says God's favor and mercy alone make purification possible, then says God purifies whom He wills; guidance is a received good rather than self-made credit.
God sends rain, brings fruit as provision, and subjects ships and rivers; these concrete gifts identify the source of the goods that the section's hamd answers.
The continuation names the sun, moon, night, and day as subjected; it completes the inventory of gifts begun in 14:32.
After the warning about denial in 14:7, this ayah says human disbelief cannot diminish God, the giver whose favor and increase are at stake.
The section names root ر ب ب for the giver; after creation, teaching, and provision, this refrain asks which of the Lord's favors the two kinds of creature will deny.
After describing human and jinn creation, this refrain makes those acts answerable as the Lord's favors, matching the section's bestowed good and recipient response.
After naming the Lord of the two easts and two wests, this question asks which of His favors can be denied; it makes created order part of the gift.
After the two seas meet yet remain separated, the refrain asks which Lord's favors are denied; the boundary between waters is the local sign in view.
After naming pearls and coral from the seas, this refrain places those specific valuables among the Lord's favors to be acknowledged.
After describing ships raised like mountains at sea, this question treats human passage across the waters as one of the Lord's favors.
After saying all on earth perishes while the Lord's face remains, the refrain asks which favors are denied; the passing and enduring boundary illuminates the section's completed gift.
After saying all in heaven and earth ask of Him and He is continually at work, this refrain identifies their dependence as a reason to acknowledge the Lord's favors.
After warning the two communities that they cannot escape God's domain, the refrain asks which favors of their Lord they deny; the gift stands beside accountability.
After challenging humans and jinn to pass beyond the heavens and earth only by authority, this question makes their limits a boundary around the Lord's favor.
After warning of fire and molten copper against the two communities, the refrain turns the judgment scene into a boundary between favor and denied response.
After the sky splits and becomes rose-like, this refrain asks which Lord's favors can be denied; it places the cosmic sign under His rule.
After saying neither human nor jinn will be asked about sin that day, the refrain asks what of their Lord's favors they deny, joining judgment to accountability.
After the guilty are recognized by their marks and seized, this refrain repeats the question of denied favors against the consequence of denial.
After describing Hell and boiling water, the refrain asks which Lord's favors are denied; the punishment supplies the explicit boundary to the section's favorable path.
After promising two gardens to the one who fears standing before the Lord, this refrain asks which favors are denied; the gardens make the promised gift concrete.
After describing gardens with many branches, this refrain counts that abundance among the Lord's favors, matching the section's image of a good completed and given.
After naming two flowing springs in the gardens, this question makes the springs a particular favor from the Lord.
After naming paired kinds of fruit in the gardens, this refrain asks which favors the recipients will deny; provision is locally explicit.
After describing reclining on garden couches, this refrain places rest and security among the Lord's gifts to the rewarded.
After describing companions untouched by human or jinn, this question counts that promised reward as a favor of the Lord.
After comparing the companions to rubies and coral, this refrain asks which favors of the Lord can be denied, with the comparison's beauty as the local gift.
After asking whether the reward of goodness is anything but goodness, this refrain links received reward to the giver's answering good.
After introducing two further gardens, this refrain identifies those gardens as favors from the Lord, a second scene of promised gift.
After describing the further gardens as dark green, this question treats their flourishing as a specific favor of the Lord.
After naming two gushing springs, this refrain makes their water another concrete favor to acknowledge.
After naming fruit, palms, and pomegranates in the gardens, this question places food among the Lord's favors.
After describing beautiful companions in the gardens, the refrain asks which favors are denied; the reward is locally specific.
After describing companions sheltered in pavilions, this refrain counts that promised shelter among the Lord's favors.
After saying the companions were untouched before by human or jinn, this question repeats the demand to acknowledge the Lord's gift.
After the final garden scene of green cushions and beautiful carpets, the refrain closes the repeated inventory by asking which of the Lord's favors can be denied.
This conclusion blesses the name of the Lord, owner of majesty and honor; it completes the refrain's inventory with praise, as the section begins with hamd to the Lord.
The section centers a favor completed and a path's guidance; this ayah names shade, shelter, and clothing, then says God completes His favor so the people may submit.
This preceding ayah names homes and animal coverings as provisions for rest and use; 16:81 completes the list by calling these gifts part of God's favor.
The section joins favor, mercy, and a straight path; this ayah promises believers mercy and bounty from God and guidance to Him on a straight path.
This ayah says revelation guides seekers of God's pleasure to paths of peace, brings them from darkness to light, and guides them to a straight path, directly joining favor to the way.
This ayah commands following God's straight path and forbids following diverging paths; it makes the boundary between the requested way and deviation explicit.
This ayah says direction of the way belongs to God while some ways diverge; it gives a specific contrast to the section's straight path and its lost way.
This ayah says the Quran guides to what is most upright and gives good news to believers who do good; it describes the path's guidance and promised outcome.
The youths ask their Lord for mercy and right direction in their affair; the prayer joins the section's two gifts, mercy and guidance.
God promises abundant spoils, restrains hostile hands, and says He guides the believers to a straight path; the ayah joins a granted benefit to guidance.
The section presents favor as good conveyed to a recipient; this ayah says God intends to bestow favor on the oppressed by making them leaders and inheritors.
This continuation says God establishes the oppressed in the land and exposes Pharaoh's feared outcome; it completes 28:5's promised favor with its concrete reversal.
Qarun's wealth is displayed as his own treasure, and he acts insolently; this opens a passage about receiving abundance while failing to credit its giver.
This ayah says to do good as God has done good to the recipient, making received favor pass onward to others, exactly the section's hand-to-hand image.
Qarun says he was given his wealth because of his own knowledge; this self-credit reverses the section's praise of the giver for the good received.
After Qarun's destruction, observers say God expands and restricts provision; this neighbor supplies the acknowledgment of God's giving that Qarun withheld.
This ayah condemns people who love praise for what they did not do; it distinguishes such self-credit from the section's hamd, which recounts a giver's actual good.
This ayah warns against exulting over what God has given and calls God no lover of boastful self-conceit; it directly bounds turning a gift into self-praise.
After Paradise's residents praise God in 39:74, this ayah depicts angels surrounding the Throne and praising their Lord; it extends the section's hamd at the path's end.
God promises full recompense to those who recite His Book and establish prayer, then زيادة from His bounty; this matches the section's dictionary sense of doing or giving more.

Among those who inherit the Book are people who wrong themselves, take a middle course, and race ahead in good by God's permission; this specifies differing responses among recipients of guidance and favor.
After Abraham's gratitude, selection, and guidance in 16:121, this ayah says God gave him good in this world and placed him among the righteous in the Hereafter.
This ayah names the earliest believers and those who follow them in goodness, God's pleasure with them, and gardens prepared for them; it gives a communal image of a favored path reaching its reward.
The parable of a grain yielding seven ears, each with many grains, depicts charity multiplied by God; it connects the section's giving of good with increase beyond the initial gift.
After 2:262 forbids reproaching a recipient, this ayah says kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, marking a boundary around genuine beneficence.

This ayah names the recipients of food—the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9 explains that the givers seek neither reward nor thanks, completing the section's image of benefit passed onward without a claim.
This ayah introduces the steep pass; the next verses define it through freeing a person and feeding vulnerable people, joining the section's path image to enacted beneficence.
The first named act on the steep pass is freeing a slave, a concrete good delivered to another along the path described in the section.
This ayah names feeding on a day of hunger as an act on the steep pass, making the section's transferred good a concrete act of provision.
The food is given to an orphan who is a relative; this ayah specifies a recipient of the beneficence on the steep pass.
This ayah adds the needy person in misery as a recipient on the steep pass, extending the concrete acts of giving in 90:13–15.
After the acts on the steep pass, this ayah names faith and mutual exhortation to patience and mercy, completing the path as shared moral practice.
This ayah identifies the denier of judgment; the following verses show the refusal of care and ostentatious worship that contradict the section's sincere response to a giver.
The denier of judgment is shown driving away an orphan, a direct reversal of the section's image of good reaching another person.
This ayah says he does not urge feeding the poor; it makes refusal of provision the opposite of the section's transferred beneficence.
The warning turns to people who pray; 107:6 identifies their prayer as display, contrasting performed piety with the section's sincere hamd and response.
This ayah describes them as heedless of their prayer; the next ayah explains the public display, distinguishing a genuine response from appearance.
These worshippers act to be seen; this directly contrasts self-display with the section's praise directed to the true giver.
They withhold even small acts of assistance, the clearest reversal of the section's good extended from one hand to another.
Men and women who give charity and lend God a good loan are promised multiplication and a noble reward; it connects the section's giving and increase to a promised return.
God made night and day for rest and seeking bounty, then asks whether people will be grateful; provision and its fitting response are explicitly joined.
God made night for rest and day for sight, yet most people are not grateful; the ayah contrasts specific gifts with their deficient response.
The ayah asks whether people distribute their Lord's mercy and says God apportions livelihood among them; it locates the giver's beneficence with God rather than its recipients.
Paradise's people praise God for removing grief from them; this directly joins the section's hamd to a received good and names what the praise answers.
The next ayah says God settled them in an enduring home by His bounty, where fatigue does not touch them; it completes 35:34's praise with the specific gift.
This parable introduces a man given two gardens with fruit, crops, and a river; the following verses show how he treats that abundance and whether he credits its giver.
The garden owner boasts to his companion that he has more wealth and stronger support; this is the section's self-display of received good in a concrete scene.
The companion asks why the owner did not attribute the garden's success to God and acknowledge that power belongs to Him; this supplies the credit to the giver absent from the owner's boast.
After the garden is destroyed, its owner regrets having associated partners with his Lord; this completes the contrast between self-confidence in 18:34 and acknowledgment of the true giver.
This command assigns relatives, the needy, and travelers their due; it makes the section's hand-to-hand delivery of good a concrete obligation.
Righteousness includes giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers; the ayah makes beneficence to recipients part of the path.
This ayah says whatever people spend, God replaces it and is the best provider; it connects a giver's outward transfer to God's provision in return.
This ayah says spending good is for the spenders themselves, who should seek God's face, and that what they spend will be repaid; it links giving to its true giver and return.
